result.markdown: --- title: "Lecture" from: markdown+emoji subtitle: "Non-linear models in `inlabru`" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: true logo: NTNU_UofG.png theme: uofg_theme.scss footer: "Back to Home" header-includes: | slide-number: "c/t" title-slide-attributes: # data-background-image: images/trondheim3.png data-background-size: cover data-background-opacity: "0.55" author: - name: Sara Martino #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: sara.martino@ntnu.no affiliations: Dept. of Mathematical Science, NTNU - name: Janine Illian #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: Janine.Illian@glasgow.ac.uk affiliations: University of Glasgow - name: Jafet Belmont #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: Jafet.Belmont@glasgow.ac.uk affiliations: University of Glasgow # date: May 22, 2025 # bibliography: references.bib embed-resources: true execute: allow-html: true freeze: auto editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ## Non linear predictor In all the models we have seen $$ \eta = \text{linear function}(\text{components}) $$ - Sometimes one is interested in models whose parameters interact in a non-linear way . . . - A simple growth model - Lee-Carter Model - Under-reported counts # A simple growth model ## A simple growth model {.smaller} We want to include some "biology" in the statistical model. The age and size of a fish have the following relationship $$ \begin{aligned} y_t&\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma^2)\\ \eta_t &= \mu_t = L(1-\exp(-k\ (t-t_0))) \end{aligned} $$ where $t$ is the age and $y_t$ the lenght of the fish Parameters are $\theta = c(L,\kappa, t_0)$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](non_linear_predictor_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## Model Parameters and Priors {.smaller} The parameters have a biological meaning and we need to assign them a prior distribution: - $L$ is the the **maximum average length** that fish approach as they become very old. $$L\sim\text{exp}(1/300)$$ In the prior $E(L) = 300$, $\text{sd}(L) = 300$ - $k$ is the the **growth rate** (how fast the fish grows) $$k\sim\text{exp}(2)$$ - $t_0$ is the the **hypothetical age at zero length** $$t_0\sim\text{exp}(1)$$ ## A simple growth model - Noisy Observations {.smaller} The age and size of a fish have the following relationship $$ \begin{aligned} y_t&\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma^2)\\ \eta_t &= \mu_t = L(1-\exp(-k\ (t-t_0))) \end{aligned} $$ where $t$ is the age and $y_t$ the lenght of the fish ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](non_linear_predictor_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ## A simple growth model ### Why do we need more than INLA? $$ \begin{aligned} y_t&\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma^2)\\ \eta_t &= \mu_t = L(1-\exp(-k\ (t-t_0))) \end{aligned} $$ **Note** This model cannot be solved in INLA...why? . . . The model components $L$, $k$, $t_0$ enter the predictor $\eta$ in a non-linear way. . . . This means that $\eta$ is **NOT** gaussian!! ## Extending INLA to non-linear predictors {.smaller} ::: smaller In addition to being a wrapper around R-INLA, inlabru extends the scope of INLA to models with non-linear predictors $\tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u})$. ::: . . . ::::::: columns :::: {.column width="70%"} ::: smaller :bulb: **The idea** :bulb: - Linearize $\tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u})$ using a first-order Taylor expansion around $\mathbf{u}_0$: $$ \tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u}) \approx \tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u}_0) + f_{\text{linear}}(\mathbf{u}) = \bar{\eta}(\mathbf{u}) $$ - Run INLA for the linearized problem\ - Iterate until convergence - $\tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u}_0))$ close enough to $\bar{\eta}(\mathbf{u_0})$ ::: :::: :::: {.column width="30%"} ::: {.callout-note .smaller} **Note** For details:\ ::: :::: ::::::: ## Extending INLA to non-linear predictors - The linearization is an approximation on top of the "usual" INLA approximation - Accuracy will depend on the nature of the non-linearity around $\mathbf{u}_0$ and the choice of convergence criteria. - Greater care than usual is needed for the choice of priors. . . . Some checks are possible (see the arxive paper)... **BUT** this method is still in an "experimental" mode, so great care is needed! ## A simple growth model - Fitting the model {.smaller} $$ \begin{align} y_t &\sim\mathcal{N}(\eta_t,\sigma^2)\\ \eta_t &= L(1-\exp(-k(t-t_0)))\\ L &\sim\exp(1/300); \qquad k \sim\exp(2);\qquad t_0\sim\exp(1) \end{align} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-2"} scale_par <- sd(df$y) df <- df %>% mutate(y_scale = y / scale_par) cmp <- ~ -1 + L(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = scale_par / 300)) + kappa(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 2)) + t0(1, -1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 1)) growth_function <- function(L, kappa, t0, age) { L * (1 - exp(-kappa * (age - t0))) } formula <- y ~ growth_function(L, kappa, t0, age) lik <- bru_obs( formula = formula, family = "gaussian", data = df ) bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 1, bru_max_iter = 20) fit <- bru(cmp, lik) ``` ::: - Scale the data (always a good practice to avoid numerical problems) ## A simple growth model - Fitting the model {.smaller} $$ \begin{align} y_t &\sim\mathcal{N}(\eta_t,\sigma^2)\\ \eta_t &= L(1-\exp(-k(t-t_0)))\\ L &\sim\exp(1/300); \qquad k \sim\exp(2);\qquad t_0\sim\exp(1) \end{align} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="3-7"} scale_par <- sd(df$y) df <- df %>% mutate(y_scale = y / scale_par) cmp <- ~ -1 + L(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = scale_par / 300)) + kappa(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 2)) + t0(1, -1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 1)) growth_function <- function(L, kappa, t0, age) { L * (1 - exp(-kappa * (age - t0))) } formula <- y ~ growth_function(L, kappa, t0, age) lik <- bru_obs( formula = formula, family = "gaussian", data = df ) bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 1, bru_max_iter = 20) fit <- bru(cmp, lik) ``` ::: - Define the components **Note** here we use the PIT transform to go from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ to $\exp(\kappa)$ This also gives a non-linear model, this "trick" can be usedful in other cases!! ## A simple growth model - Fitting the model {.smaller} $$ \begin{align} y_t &\sim\mathcal{N}(\eta_t,\sigma^2)\\ \eta_t &= L(1-\exp(-k(t-t_0)))\\ L &\sim\exp(1/300); \qquad k \sim\exp(2);\qquad t_0\sim\exp(1) \end{align} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="9-13"} scale_par <- sd(df$y) df <- df %>% mutate(y_scale = y / scale_par) cmp <- ~ -1 + L(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = scale_par / 300)) + kappa(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 2)) + t0(1, -1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 1)) growth_function <- function(L, kappa, t0, age) { L * (1 - exp(-kappa * (age - t0))) } formula <- y ~ growth_function(L, kappa, t0, age) lik <- bru_obs( formula = formula, family = "gaussian", data = df ) bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 1, bru_max_iter = 20) fit <- bru(cmp, lik) ``` ::: - Define the non-linear function of the paramters and the formula ## A simple growth model - Fitting the model {.smaller} $$ \begin{align} y_t &\sim\mathcal{N}(\eta_t,\sigma^2)\\ \eta_t &= L(1-\exp(-k(t-t_0)))\\ L &\sim\exp(1/300); \qquad k \sim\exp(2);\qquad t_0\sim\exp(1) \end{align} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="15-22"} scale_par <- sd(df$y) df <- df %>% mutate(y_scale = y / scale_par) cmp <- ~ -1 + L(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = scale_par / 300)) + kappa(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 2)) + t0(1, -1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 1)) growth_function <- function(L, kappa, t0, age) { L * (1 - exp(-kappa * (age - t0))) } formula <- y ~ growth_function(L, kappa, t0, age) lik <- bru_obs( formula = formula, family = "gaussian", data = df ) bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 1, bru_max_iter = 20) fit <- bru(cmp, lik) ``` ::: - Define the likelihood and the run the model as usual **NOTE** the `bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 1, bru_max_iter = 20)` is a way to get some infor out of the `bru()` function ## ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` bru: Preprocessing ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Iteration 1 [max: 20] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Iteration 2 [max: 20] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Max deviation from previous: 11000% of SD, and line search is active [stop if: < 10% and line search inactive] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Iteration 3 [max: 20] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Max deviation from previous: 892% of SD, and line search is active [stop if: < 10% and line search inactive] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Iteration 4 [max: 20] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Max deviation from previous: 1.87% of SD, and line search is inactive [stop if: < 10% and line search inactive] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Convergence criterion met. Running final INLA integration step with known theta mode. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` iinla: Iteration 5 [max: 20] ``` ::: ::: ## Checking results - Estimated parameters ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](non_linear_predictor_slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: # Lee-Carter Model ## A (Bayesian) spatial extention of the Lee-Carter model {.smaller} $$\begin{align*} Y_{xt} \mid \lambda_{xt} &\sim \text{Poisson}(E_{xt} \lambda_{xt})\\ \log(\lambda_{xts}) &= \alpha_x + \beta_x \kappa_t + \omega_{sg_x} + z_{xts} \end{align*} $$ with - $\alpha_x \mid \tau_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_\alpha)$, for $x=1, \ldots, N$. - $\beta_x \mid \tau_\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_\beta)$, for $x=1, \ldots, N$, with $\sum_x \beta_x = 1$ - $\kappa_t = \phi \cdot t + \kappa^\star_{t}\$, $\ t=1, \ldots, T$, where ${\kappa}^\star$ follows a RW1($\tau_\kappa$) and $\sum \kappa_t = 0$ - $\omega_{sg_x} \mid \tau_\omega$ Age specific spatial effect - $z_{xts} \mid \tau_z$ iid effect to allow for extra variability ## Identifiability Constraints Model is not unique: $$\alpha_x + \beta_x \kappa_t = \alpha_x + (c \beta_x)(\kappa_t / c)$$ So we impose constraints: - $\sum_t \kappa_t = 0$ - $\sum_x \beta_x = 1$ :point_right: Ensures unique interpretation of parameters ## `inlabru` implementation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp_model1 = ~ -1 + alpha(age,model= "iid", constr = F,)+ beta(age, model= "iid", extraconstr = list(A=A, e=e))+ kappa(time, model= "rw2", constr = T) + spatial(space, model = "bym2", graph = Q_space, replicate = as.numeric(as.factor(age2)), nrep = length(unique(df$age2))) + random(rand2, model = "iid") formula_model = Y ~ Intercept + subgraphs + alpha + beta * kappa + spatial + random likelihood = bru_obs(formula = formula_model, family = "poisson", data = df , E = E) result_model = bru(components = cmp_model, likelihood) ``` ::: $$ \log(\lambda_{xts}) = \alpha_x + \beta_x \kappa_t + \omega_{sg_x} + z_{xts} $$ ## Results ![](images/clipboard-2457513482.png) # Accounting for underreporting ## Model for underreported counts The true (unobserved ) counts $$ \begin{align} Y^*_i & \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i\lambda_i)\\ \log(\lambda_i) & = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + u_i \end{align} $$ . . . The thinned (observed ) counts $$ \begin{aligned} Y_i & \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i\lambda_i\pi_i)\\ \log(\lambda_i) & = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + u_i\\ \text{logit}(\pi_i)& = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1z_i\\ \end{aligned} $$ . . . The non-linear predictor $$ \begin{align} Y_i & \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i\lambda_i\pi_i)\\ \eta_i & = \log(\lambda_i\pi_i) \\ & = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + u_i + \log(\text{inv.logit}(\alpha_0 + \alpha_1z_i)) \end{align} $$ ## `inlabru` implementation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} func_probs = function(v,alpha0,alpha1) { aa = alpha0 + alpha1 * v return(-log(1+exp(-aa))) } cmp = ~ -1 + beta_0(main = 1, model = "linear") + beta_1(main = covariate_x, model = "linear")+ spatial(loc, model = "besag", graph = Q) + alpha_0(main = 1, model = "linear", mean.linear = b0_mean, prec.linear = 1/(b0_sd)^2) + alpha_1(main = 1, model = "linear") formula = Y_obs ~ beta_0 + beta_1 + spatial + func(covariate_z, b0, b1) lik1 = bru_obs("poisson", formula = formula, data= df, E = E) fit1 <- bru(cmp, lik) ``` ::: **NOTE** we have (quite) informative priors for $\alpha_0$ ## Final Notes - Be careful when using this models!!! - Think carefully if the model makes sense - Think carefully about priors - Check the convergence ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 2) ``` :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
